\label{th:3}
Let $\prec$ be the same total order on $W$ as in Theorem \ref{th:1}, 
and let $\mathcal D=\mathop{\mathrm D\kern0pt}\nolimits^b (\mathop{\sf {Coh}}\nolimits( \mathbf G/\mathbf B))$. Let $v,w$ denote elements of  $W$. Then there are objects ${\mathcal X}_v\in \mathcal D$ such that 
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\mathop{\mathrm {Hom}}\nolimits_{\mathcal D}({\mathcal X}_v,{\mathcal X}_v[i])=\begin{cases}{\sf k} &\text{if $i=0$}\\
0&\text{else.}\end{cases}$.

\

\

\item If $w\succ  v$ then $\mathop{\mathrm {Hom}}\nolimits_{\mathcal D}({\mathcal X}_v,{\mathcal X}_w[i])=0$ for all $i$.\\
\item The triangulated hull of $\{{\mathcal X}_v\mid v \in W\}$ is $\mathcal D$.
\end{enumerate}
In other words, the collection of objects $({\mathcal X}_v)_{v \in W}$ is a full exceptional collection in $ \mathcal D$.

\label{th:universal coefficients}
Let ${\sf k}$ be a Dedekind ring and let $\mathbf G$ be an affine algebraic group, flat over ${\sf k}$. Let ${\sf k}'$ be commutative ${\sf k}$-algebra and $n\geq0$.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item There is for any $\mathbf G$-module $M$, flat over ${\sf k}$, an exact sequence
    $$0\to H^n(\mathbf G,M)\otimes {\sf k}'\to H^n(\mathbf G_{{\sf k}'},M)\to \mathrm{Tor}_1^{\sf k}(H^{n+1}(G,M),{\sf k}')\to 0.$$
    \item Let  $X$ be a closed reduced
    $\mathbb B_{\sf k}$-invariant subscheme, flat over ${\sf k}$, of the generalized flag variety $(\mathbb G/\mathbb P)_{\sf k}$. For any  $\mathbb P_{\sf k}$-module $N$, finitely generated and flat over ${\sf k}$, we have an exact 
    sequence 
    \end{enumerate}
    $$0\to H^n(X,\mathcal L(N))\otimes {\sf k}'\to H^n(X_{{\sf k}'},\mathcal L(N))\to \mathrm{Tor}_1^{\sf k}(H^{n+1}(X,\mathcal L(N),{\sf k}')\to 0,$$
where $\mathcal L(N)$ is the vector bundle associated to $N$ 
    (\cite[I 5.8]{Jan}).

nodes.raw_latex:
\label{lem:Schubert module}
    Let $S, S'$ be  unions of Schubert varieties  in $ \mathbf G /{\mathbf B}$ and let $\lambda$ be dominant. 
\begin{itemize}\item The extremal weights of $\Gamma(S,\mathcal L(\lambda))$ are the $w\lambda$ 
with $wx_-\in S$.
\item  $\Gamma(\mathbf G/\mathbf B,\mathcal L(\lambda))\to\Gamma(S,\mathcal L(\lambda))$ is surjective.
\item If $S'\subset S$, then $\Gamma(S,\mathcal L(\lambda))\to\Gamma(S',\mathcal L(\lambda))$ is surjective, and its kernel has a relative Schubert filtration.
\item $H^i(S,\mathcal L(\lambda))=0$ for $i>0$.
\end{itemize}

nodes.statement: We may assume sf k=mathbb C, because of the base change properties of the Q(mu). Suppose Q(-mu) is larger than its socle sf k_-mu. Let nu be a weight of the socle of Q(-mu)/sf k_-mu and let f be a nonzero weight vector of Q(-mu), of weight nu, mapping to a vector of the socle of Q(-mu)/sf k_-mu. As the socle of Q(-mu) is its weight space sf k_-mu, the vector f can not be fixed by the unipotent radical mathbf U of mathbf B. But it is well known that mathbf U(mathbb C) is generated by the x_-alpha(t) with alpha simple. So there must be such an x_-alpha(t) with x_-alpha(t)(f)-f a nonzero vector in sf k_-mu. In particular, -mu=nu + n(-alpha) for some integer n. But nu must be strictly shorter than the unique extremal weight -mu of Q(-mu). However, there is no strictly shorter weight in -mu +mathbb Zalpha.

We may assume ${\sf k}={\mathbb C}$, because of the base change properties \cite[Chapter 7]{WvdKTata} of the $Q(\mu)$.
 Suppose $Q(-\mu)$ is larger than its socle ${\sf k}_{-\mu}$. Let $\nu$ be a weight of the socle of $Q(-\mu)/{\sf k}_{-\mu}$
 and let $f$ be a nonzero weight vector of $Q(-\mu)$, of weight $\nu$, 
 mapping to a vector of the socle of $Q(-\mu)/{\sf k}_{-\mu}$.
 As the socle of $Q(-\mu)$ is its weight space ${\sf k}_{-\mu}$, the vector  $f$ can not be fixed by the unipotent radical $\mathbf U$
 of $\mathbf B$. But it is well known
 that  $\mathbf U({\mathbb C})$ is generated by the $x_{-\alpha}(t)$ with $\alpha$ simple. So there must be such an $x_{-\alpha}(t)$ with 
 $x_{-\alpha}(t)(f)-f$ a nonzero vector in ${\sf k}_{-\mu}$. In particular, $-\mu=\nu + n(-\alpha)$ for some integer $n$. But $\nu$
 must be strictly shorter than the unique extremal weight $-\mu$ of $Q(-\mu)$. However, there is no strictly shorter 
 weight in $-\mu +{\mathbb Z}\alpha$.

 The extremal weights of $\Gamma(\overline{{\mathbf B}w_0x_-},\mathcal L(-w_0ve_v))$ are the elements in the $W$ orbit of $-w_0ve_v$,
 hence of $-ve_v$.
 Now suppose $-ve_v$ is  an extremal weight of $\Gamma((\partial \overline{{\mathbf B}v{\mathbf B}})\;\overline{{\mathbf B}v^{-1}w_0x_-},\mathcal L(-w_0ve_v))$.
Then $-ve_v$ can be written as $y(-w_0ve_v)$ with $y\leq z\star v^{-1}w_0$ for some $z<v$.
Replacing $z$ by a lesser element if necessary, we may assume $y\leq zv^{-1}w_0$ for some $z<v$.
Put $u=yw_0$. Then $-ve_v=-uve_v$ with $u\geq zv^{-1}$. But $-ve_v=-uve_v$ implies $u\in W_I$, so 
$u\geq zv^{-1}$ implies $zv^{-1}\in W_I$. Thus $z^{-1}\in v^{-1}W_I$.
This contradicts the minimality of $v^{-1}$ in its coset $v^{-1}W_I$.

Part (2). Now consider a weight of the form $-uve_v$ with $-uve_v\neq -ve_v$. We may replace $u$ by its minimal coset representative.
As $\ell(u)\geq 1$ there is a simple reflection $s$ with $s\notin I$ and $\ell(u)= \ell(us)+1$. In particular, $u\geq s$.
Now $v^{-1}s<v^{-1}$ by the construction of $e_v$. Put $z=sv$, $y=uw_0$. Then $z<v$, $-uve_v=y(-w_0ve_v)$, with
$y\leq sw_0=z\star v^{-1}w_0$.

both parts go through when ${\sf k}={\mathbb Z}$ or when ${\sf k}$ is a field of characteristic zero.

Proof of part \ref{Leray3}. By the previous parts the result holds when $S$ is a Schubert variety. 
There are only finitely many possibilities for $S$, so we may assume the result for any union of Schubert varieties that is
strictly contained in $S$. If $S$ is not a Schubert variety, write $S=S'\cup S''$ where $S'$, $S''$ are strictly smaller.
Put $X=\overline{{\mathbf B}w{\mathbf B}}/\mathbf B$
and $M=H^0(X,\mathcal L(\lambda))$.
If ${\sf k}$ is a field of finite characteristic, then $S'\cap S''$ is reduced by Ramanathan \cite[Proposition 1.2.1, Chapter 2]{BK}. By \cite[Corollary 1.6.6]{BK}
it is then also reduced in characteristic zero.
From the Mayer--Vietoris sequence 
$$0\to  H^0(S,\mathcal L(M))\to H^0(S',\mathcal L(M))\oplus H^0(S'',\mathcal L(M))\to H^0(S'\cap S'',\mathcal L(M))\to\cdots$$
we get
\begin{equation}\label{eq:chiM}
    \chi(S,\mathcal L(M))=\chi(S',\mathcal L(M))+\chi(S'',\mathcal L(M))- \chi(S'\cap S'',\mathcal L(M)).
\end{equation}

$$0\to H^0(\tilde SX ,\mathcal L(\lambda))\to H^0(\tilde S'X ,\mathcal L(\lambda))\oplus H^0(\tilde S''X ,\mathcal L(\lambda))\to H^0(\tilde S'X\cap \tilde S''X ,\mathcal L(\lambda))\to0,$$

.\end{equation}
By Lemma \ref{lem:capw} we know that $\tilde S'X\cap \tilde S''X =(\tilde S'\cap \tilde S'')X $.
As the right hand sides of equations (\ref{eq:chiM}), (\ref{eq:chilambda})
agree, part \ref{Leray3} follows.

($\Leftarrow$). Assume given $M\in {\sf A}$, $N\in {\sf B}$ and assume ${\mathrm{Rind}}_{ \mathbf P}^{ \mathbf G}(N^{\ast}\otimes _k M)=0$.

\begin{eqnarray*}&\mathop{\mathrm {RHom}}\nolimits _{\mathop{\mathrm D\kern0pt}\nolimits ^{b}({\mathrm{rep}}( \mathbf P))}(N,M)=\mathop{\mathrm {RHom}}\nolimits _{\mathop{\mathrm D\kern0pt}\nolimits ^{b}({\mathrm{rep}}( \mathbf P))}({\sf k},N^*\otimes M)=\\
&\mathop{\mathrm {RHom}}\nolimits _{\mathop{\mathrm D\kern0pt}\nolimits ^{b}({\mathrm{rep}}(\mathbf G))}({\sf k},{\mathrm{Rind}}_{ \mathbf P}^{ \mathbf G}(N^{\ast}\otimes _k M))=0.
\end{eqnarray*}

($\Rightarrow$). Let $M\in {\sf A}$, $N\in {\sf B}$ and 
$\mathop{\mathrm {RHom}}\nolimits _{\mathop{\mathrm D\kern0pt}\nolimits ^{b}({\mathrm{rep}}( \mathbf P))}(N,M)=0$ for all such $M$, $N$.
Let be $L$ an arbitrary object of $\mathop{\mathrm D\kern0pt}\nolimits ^{b}({\mathrm{rep}}( \mathbf G))$. Then 
$$

$$
and 
$$
\mathop{\mathrm {RHom}}\nolimits _{\mathop{\mathrm D\kern0pt}\nolimits ^{b}({\mathrm{rep}}( \mathbf P))}({\mathrm{res}} _{ \mathbf P}^{ \mathbf G}L,N^{\ast}\otimes _{{\sf k}}M)
=\mathop{\mathrm {RHom}}\nolimits _{\mathop{\mathrm D\kern0pt}\nolimits ^{b}({\mathrm{rep}}( \mathbf P))}(N\otimes _{{\sf k}}{\mathrm{res}} _{ \mathbf P}^{ \mathbf G}L,M)=0;

First we show that ${\mathrm{rep}}(\mathbf G)$ lies in the subcategory.
We choose a real valued additive injective height function ${\mathrm {ht}}$ on the weight lattice which is positive on positive roots.
Consider a nonzero $M\in{\mathrm{rep}}( \mathbf G)$. Say $\mu$ is its highest weight with respect to ${\mathrm {ht}}$. 
Thus ${\mathrm {ht}}(\mu)\geq0$. Assume that all representations with a smaller highest weight are in the subcategory. We have a map $\Delta_\mu\to \nabla_\mu$ whose kernel and cokernel have
lower weights, so  $\Delta_\mu$ lies in the subcategory.
Let $M_{\mu,\mathrm {triv}}$ denote the weight space $M_{\mu}$ provided with a trivial $ \mathbf G$ action.
By \cite[Proposition 21]{FvdK} there is a natural map 
$\Delta_\mu\otimes_{\sf k} M_{\mu,\mathrm {triv}}\to M$ whose kernel and cokernel have lower weights.  
Now notice that $\Delta_\mu\otimes_{\sf k} M_{\mu,\mathrm {triv}}$ lies in the subcategory. So $M$ does too.
So ${\mathrm{rep}}(\mathbf G)$ lies in the subcategory. 
Now use that every object of $\mathop{\mathrm D\kern0pt}\nolimits^b({\mathrm{rep}}(\mathbf G))$  is quasi-isomorphic to a bounded complex in ${\mathrm{rep}}( \mathbf G)$ and that bounded complexes are repeated cones of pure objects. (cf.\ ``Stupid  truncations'' \cite[2.5]{Kuzbasech}.)

\label{prop:touch}
  Let $\lambda$ be a weight in the $W$ orbit of the dominant weight $\varpi$. 
  Assume $\alpha_i^\vee(\varpi)\leq1$ for all
  simple $\alpha_i$. 
  Take $w$ minimal so that $\lambda=w\varpi$. Let there be an $\alpha_j$  such that $\alpha_j^\vee(\varpi)=1$ and

  So $\mu\leq_a\lambda$.

nodes.name: \rm \bf  Proof of Theorem \ref{th:generation}
nodes.statement: Let varpi be dominant and let lambda be a weight in its W orbit. Choose w minimal so that lambda=wvarpi. Assume that for all vgeq w with vvarpineq lambda the representation e^vvarpi is in the subcategory. Assume also that for all weights mu with (mu,mu)<(lambda,lambda) the one dimensional representation e^mu of weight mu is in the subcategory. In other words, assume that e^mu is in the subcategory for all mu with mu<_alambda. We claim that then e^lambda is in the subcategory. The theorem easily follows from the claim by induction along <_a. So let us prove the claim. There are several cases. If lambda is a Steinberg weight e_v, then one uses the given properties of M_v. So we may assume it is not a Steinberg weight. There are two cases. The first case is that alpha_i^vee(varpi)leq 1 for all i. As lambda is not a Steinberg weight there must be a j with alpha_j^vee(varpi)=1 but w(alpha_j) positive. Then ell(ws_j)>ell(w) and we are in the situation of Proposition . Let tau=varpi-omega_j. Then tau is strictly shorter than lambda, so e^wtau is in our subcategory, and therefore N=e^wtauotimes nabla(omega_j) is in the subcategory. The weights mu of N lie in the convex hull of wtau+Womega_j and are either shorter than lambda or they are of the form vvarpi with vgeq w. That is muleq_alambda. So e^mu is in the subcategory for all weights of N different from lambda and lambda has multiplicity one in N. It follows that e^lambda is in the subcategory. The second case is that some alpha_j^vee(varpi)> 1. Put tau=varpi-omega_j. Again tau is strictly shorter than varpi. By Proposition the weights mu of N=e^wtauotimes nabla(omega_j) are either shorter than lambda or they are of the form vvarpi with vgeq w. So e^mu is in the subcategory for all weights of N different from lambda and lambda has multiplicity one in N. It follows that e^lambda is in the subcategory.

Let $\varpi$ be dominant and let $\lambda$ be a weight in its $W$ orbit. Choose $w$ minimal so that 
  $\lambda=w\varpi$.
  Assume that for all $v\geq w$ with $v\varpi\neq \lambda$ the representation $e^{v\varpi}$ 
   is in the subcategory.
Assume also that for all weights $\mu$ with $(\mu,\mu)<(\lambda,\lambda)$ 
  the one dimensional representation $e^\mu$ of weight $\mu$ is in the subcategory. 
  In other words, assume that $e^\mu$  is in the subcategory for all $\mu$ with $\mu<_a\lambda$.
  
  We claim that then    $e^\lambda$ is in the subcategory.
  The theorem easily follows from the claim by induction along $<_a$.
  
  So let us prove the claim.
  
  There are several cases.
  
  If $\lambda$ is a Steinberg weight $e_v$, then one uses the given properties of $M_v$.
  
  So we may assume it is not a Steinberg weight.
   
  There are two cases.
  
  The first case is that $\alpha_i^\vee(\varpi)\leq 1$ for all $i$.
  As $\lambda$ is not a Steinberg weight there must be a $j$ with $\alpha_j^\vee(\varpi)=1$ but $w(\alpha_j)$ positive.
 Then $\ell(ws_j)>\ell(w)$ and we are in the situation of Proposition \ref{prop:touch}. 
 Let $\tau=\varpi-\omega_j$. Then $\tau$ is strictly shorter than $\lambda$, so $e^{w\tau}$ is in our subcategory, and therefore
  $N=e^{w\tau}\otimes \nabla(\omega_j)$ is in the subcategory. The weights $\mu$ of $N$  lie in the convex hull of $w\tau+W\omega_j$ and are either shorter than $\lambda$
  or they are of the form $v\varpi$ with $v\geq w$. That is $\mu\leq_a\lambda$.
  So $e^\mu$ is in the subcategory for all weights of $N$ different from $\lambda$ and $\lambda$ has multiplicity one in $N$. It follows that $e^\lambda$ is in the subcategory.
  
  The second case is that some $\alpha_j^\vee(\varpi)> 1$. Put $\tau=\varpi-\omega_j$. Again $\tau$ is strictly shorter than $\varpi$.
  By Proposition \ref{prop:fartouch}
  the weights  $\mu$ of $N=e^{w\tau}\otimes \nabla(\omega_j)$ are either shorter than $\lambda$
  or they are of the form $v\varpi$ with $v\geq w$.
 So $e^\mu$ is in the subcategory for all weights of $N$ different from $\lambda$ and $\lambda$ has multiplicity one in $N$. It follows that $e^\lambda$ is in the subcategory.

nodes.statement: If sigma is not a Steinberg weight, then there is a fundamental weight omega_j and a weight mu with (mu,mu)<(sigma,sigma), so that the mathbf B-module L=nabla_omega_jotimes e^mu has sigma as a weight of multiplicity one, and so that all weights nu of L satisfy nuleq_asigma.
assumptions: If sigma is not a Steinberg weight
conclusions: then there is a fundamental weight omega_j and a weight mu with (mu,mu)<(sigma,sigma), so that the mathbf B-module L=nabla_omega_jotimes e^mu has sigma as a weight of multiplicity one, and so that all weights nu of L satisfy nuleq_asigma.
nodes.raw_latex:
\label{cor:if not Steinberg then tensor}
If $\sigma$ is not a Steinberg weight, then  
 there is a fundamental weight $\omega_j$ and a weight $\mu$ with $(\mu,\mu)<(\sigma,\sigma)$,
 so that the $\mathbf B$-module $L=\nabla_{\omega_j}\otimes e^\mu$  has
$\sigma$ as a weight  of  multiplicity one, and so that all weights  $\nu$ of $L$ satisfy 
$\nu\leq_a\sigma$.

nodes.statement: We adapt the proof of Theorem . First let us rephrase what we need to show. We need to show that if mu<_alambda, then e^mu is in the triangulated hull of \nabla_nuotimes M_vmid nuin X( mathbf T)_+,~vin W, ~e_v<_alambda\. By Proposition this hull is mathbf G-linear. We want to show by induction along <_a that e^mu is in the hull. So assume e^sigma is in the hull for sigma<_amu. There are two cases: mu is a Steinberg weight or it is not. If it is a Steinberg weight, then it is an e_v with e_v<_alambda. And all weights sigma of M_v that are distinct from mu=e_v satisfy sigma<_amu. If mu is not a Steinberg weight, then by Corollary there is a module N in \nabla_nuotimes e^taumid nuin X( mathbf T)_+,~(tau,tau)<(mu,mu)\ with mu a weight of N of multiplicity one, and all weights sigma of N satisfying sigmaleq_amu. But (tau,tau)<(mu,mu) implies tau<_amu.
nodes.raw_latex:
We adapt the proof of Theorem \ref{th:generation}. First let us rephrase what we need to show. We need to show that if $\mu<_a\lambda$, then $e^\mu$ is in the triangulated hull of 

$\{\nabla_\nu\otimes M_v\mid \nu\in X( \mathbf T)_+,~v\in W, ~e_v<_a\lambda\}.$
By  Proposition \ref{prop:G linear hull} this hull is $\mathbf G$-linear.
We want to show by induction along $<_a$ that $e^\mu$ is in the  hull.
 So assume $e^\sigma$ is in the hull for $\sigma<_a\mu$.

There are two cases: $\mu$ is a Steinberg weight or it is not. If it is a Steinberg weight, then it is an $e_v$ with $e_v<_a\lambda$. And all weights $\sigma$ of $M_v$ that are distinct from $\mu=e_v$ satisfy $\sigma<_a\mu$.
If $\mu$ is not a Steinberg weight, then by Corollary \ref{cor:if not Steinberg then tensor} there is a module $N$  in  $\{\nabla_\nu\otimes e^\tau\mid \nu\in X( \mathbf T)_+,~(\tau,\tau)<(\mu,\mu)\}$ 
with $\mu$ a weight  of $N$ of multiplicity one, and all weights  $\sigma$ of $N$ satisfying 
$\sigma\leq_a\mu$. But $(\tau,\tau)<(\mu,\mu)$ implies $\tau<_a\mu$.

$(1).$ Recall that for $p\in W$, the object $X_p$ is both the projection of $P(-e_v)^*$ onto the category ${\sf Q}_{\succeq p}$ and the projection of $Q(e_p)$ onto ${\sf P}_{\preceq p}$. 
Tensoring the triangles (\ref{eq:def_triang_X_p}) and (\ref{eq:def_triang_Y_p}) with modules $M$ and $N$, respectively, we get:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:otimesM}
\dots \rightarrow M\otimes P(-e_p)^*\rightarrow M\otimes X_p\rightarrow M\otimes {\sf cone}(P(-e_p)^*\rightarrow X_p)\rightarrow \dots 
\end{equation}
and 
\begin{equation}\label{eq:otimesN}
\dots \rightarrow N\otimes X_p\rightarrow N\otimes Q(e_p)\rightarrow N\otimes {\sf cone}(X_p\rightarrow Q(e_p))\rightarrow \dots 
\end{equation}
We have that ${\sf cone}(P(-e_p)^*\rightarrow X_p)\in {\sf P}_{\prec p}$ and ${\sf cone}(X_p\rightarrow Q(e_p))\in {\sf Q}_{\succ p}$, and both subcategories ${\sf P}_{\prec p}$ and ${\sf Q}_{\succ p}$ are $ \mathbf G$-linear, thus also
$M\otimes {\sf cone}(P(-e_p)^*\rightarrow X_p)\in {\sf P}_{\prec p}$ and $N\otimes {\sf cone}(X_p\rightarrow Q(e_p))\in {\sf Q}_{\succ p}$. 

We have $\mathop{\mathrm {Hom}}\nolimits _{\mathcal D}(M\otimes {\sf cone}(P(-e_p)^*\rightarrow X_p),N\otimes X_p[i]))=0$ for all $i$ since $X_p\in {\sf Q}_{\succeq p}\cap {\sf P}_{\preceq p}\subset {\sf Q}_{\succeq p}$ and ${\sf Q}_{\succeq p}={\sf P}_{\prec p}^{\perp}$ by 
 (\ref{eq:p-q-SOD-2}). Applying $\mathop{\mathrm {Hom}}\nolimits _{\mathcal D}(-,N\otimes X_p)$ to the triangle (\ref{eq:otimesM}), we then obtain $\mathop{\mathrm {Hom}}\nolimits _{\mathcal D}(M\otimes X_p,N\otimes X_p[i])=\mathop{\mathrm {Hom}}\nolimits _{\mathcal D}(M\otimes P(-e_p)^*,N\otimes X_p[i])$ for all $i$.
 
Next, we have $\mathop{\mathrm {Hom}}\nolimits _{\mathcal D}(M\otimes X_p,N\otimes {\sf cone}(X_p\rightarrow Q(e_p)[i]))=0$ for all $i$ since $X_p\in {\sf Q}_{\succeq p}\cap {\sf P}_{\preceq p}\subset {\sf P}_{\preceq p}$ and ${\sf Q}_{\succ p}={\sf P}_{\preceq p}^{\perp}$ by 
 (\ref{eq:p-q-SOD-1}). Applying $\mathop{\mathrm {Hom}}\nolimits _{\mathcal D}(M\otimes X_p,-)$ to the triangle (\ref{eq:otimesN}), we then obtain $\mathop{\mathrm {Hom}}\nolimits _{\mathcal D}(M\otimes P(-e_p)^*,N\otimes X_p[i])=\mathop{\mathrm {Hom}}\nolimits _{\mathcal D}(M\otimes P(-e_p)^*,N\otimes Q(e_p)[i])$ for all $i$. The latter group is isomorphic to ${\mathrm{Ext}} ^i_{\mathbf B}(M\otimes P(-e_p)^*,N\otimes Q(e_p))$. Now the statement in (1) follows by Corollary \ref{cor:left orthogonal}, (1).



$(2).$ The second part follows similarly using Corollary \ref{cor:left orthogonal}, (2).

\label{th:coh-semi-orthogonal}Let $\mathcal D=\mathop{\mathrm D\kern0pt}\nolimits^b (\mathbf G/\mathbf B)$.
Let $v,w\in W$.\\
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\mathop{\mathrm {Hom}}\nolimits_{\mathcal D}({\mathcal X}_v,{\mathcal X}_v[i])=\begin{cases}{\sf k} &\text{if $i=0$},\\
0&\text{else.}\end{cases}$\\

\

\item If $w\succ  v$ then $\mathop{\mathrm {Hom}}\nolimits_{\mathcal D}({\mathcal X}_v,{\mathcal X}_w[i])=0$ for all $i$.\\
\item The triangulated hull of $\{{\mathcal X}_v\mid v \in W\}$ is $\mathcal D$.
\end{enumerate}

$(1)$. By Proposition \ref{prop:derived_B-cohomology}, the functor 
$\mathop{\mathrm {RHom}}\nolimits _{ \mathbf G/\mathbf B}(\mathcal L (-),\mathcal L (-))$ canonically factors through ${\mathrm{Rind}} _{\mathbf B}^{ \mathbf G}((-)^{\ast}\otimes (-))$
and $\mathop{\mathrm {RHom}}\nolimits_{\mathcal D}({\mathcal X}_v,{\mathcal X}_v)=\mathop{\mathrm {RHom}}\nolimits _{ \mathbf G/\mathbf B}(\mathcal L (X_v),\mathcal L (X_v))={\sf For}\circ {\mathrm{Rind}}_{\mathbf B}^{ \mathbf G}(X_v^{\ast}\otimes X_v)$ where $\sf For$ is the forgetful functor $\mathop{\mathrm D\kern0pt}\nolimits ^b({\mathrm{rep}}( \mathbf G))\rightarrow \mathop{\mathrm D\kern0pt}\nolimits ^b( {{\sf k}\textrm{-}\mathrm{mod}})$. This also holds when ${\sf k}={\mathbb Z}$.
Now by Corollary \ref{cor:Rind_B^G(X_p*otimesX_p)} (1), ${\mathrm{Rind}}_{\mathbf B}^{ \mathbf G}(X_v^{\ast}\otimes X_v)={\sf k}$. 



$(2)$. This is the same argument as in (1), using Corollary \ref{cor:Rind_B^G(X_p*otimesX_p)} (2).





$(3).$  We 
will prove that 
the 
triangulated hull $\langle {\mathcal X}_v, v\in W\rangle$ of $\{{\mathcal X}_v, v\in W\}$ in $\mathcal D=\mathop{\mathrm D\kern0pt}\nolimits^b (\mathop{\sf {Coh}}\nolimits( \mathbf G/\mathbf B))$
is the whole $\mathop{\mathrm D\kern0pt}\nolimits^b (\mathop{\sf {Coh}}\nolimits( \mathbf G/\mathbf B))$. Observe that by the previous items (1) and (2), the collection of ${\mathcal X}_v, v\in W$ is exceptional. 
Thus,  $\langle {\mathcal X}_v, v\in W\rangle\subset \mathop{\mathrm D\kern0pt}\nolimits^b (\mathop{\sf {Coh}}\nolimits( \mathbf G/\mathbf B))$ is an admissible (hence thick) subcategory of $\mathop{\mathrm D\kern0pt}\nolimits^b (\mathop{\sf {Coh}}\nolimits( \mathbf G/\mathbf B))$, see Section \ref{sec:rappel_triangulated}. We are bound to show that $\langle{\mathcal X}_v, v\in W\rangle^{\perp}=0$. Let us show that $\langle {\mathcal X}_v, v\in W\rangle$ contains the category $\mathop{\mathrm D\kern0pt}\nolimits ^b_{ \mathbf G}( \mathbf G/ \mathbf B):=\mathop{\mathrm D\kern0pt}\nolimits ^b({\sf Coh}^{ \mathbf G}( \mathbf G/ \mathbf B))$
of all $ \mathbf G$-equivariant objects of $\mathop{\mathrm D\kern0pt}\nolimits^b (\mathop{\sf {Coh}}\nolimits( \mathbf G/\mathbf B))$. 

By Lemma \ref{lem:samehull},  ${\mathrm{hull}}(\{\nabla_\lambda\otimes X_v\}_{v\in W})$ coincides with the hull of ${\mathrm{rep}}( \mathbf B)$ in $\mathop{\mathrm D\kern0pt}\nolimits^b ({\mathrm{rep}} ({\mathbf B}))$. 
In particular, the abelian category ${\mathrm{rep}}( \mathbf B)\subset \mathop{\mathrm D\kern0pt}\nolimits^b ({\mathrm{rep}} ({\mathbf B}))$ is contained in  ${\mathrm{hull}}(\{\nabla_{\lambda}\otimes X_v\}_{v\in W})$. 
By definition, ${\mathcal X}_v=\mathcal L (X_v)$; applying the functor $\mathcal L$ to the above inclusion, we see that the category of $ \mathbf G$-equivariant coherent sheaves ${\sf Coh}^{ \mathbf G}( \mathbf G/ \mathbf B)=\mathcal L ({\mathrm{rep}}( \mathbf B))$ is contained in the image under 
$\mathcal L$ of  ${\mathrm{hull}}(\{\nabla_{\lambda}\otimes X_v\}_{v\in W})$. 
Recall that the functor $\mathcal L$ is monoidal; thus, $\mathcal L (\nabla_{\lambda}\otimes X_v)=\mathcal L (\nabla_{\lambda})\otimes{\mathcal X}_v$. 
Now $\mathcal L (\nabla_{\lambda})$ is a ($ \mathbf G$-equivariant) trivial vector bundle on $ \mathbf G/ \mathbf B$, so the image of 
${\mathrm{hull}}(\{\nabla_{\lambda}\otimes X_v\}_{v\in W})$ under $\mathcal L$ coincides with the hull $\langle {\mathcal X}_v, v\in W\rangle$ of $\{ {\mathcal X}_v, v\in W\}$. 
We conclude that $\langle {\mathcal X}_v, v\in W\rangle$ contains the category $\mathop{\mathrm D\kern0pt}\nolimits ^b_{ \mathbf G}( \mathbf G/ \mathbf B)$.

Now since $\mathop{\mathrm D\kern0pt}\nolimits ^b_{ \mathbf G}( \mathbf G/ \mathbf B)\subset \langle {\mathcal X}_v, v\in W\rangle$, the  category $\langle {\mathcal X}_v, v\in W\rangle$
contains all line bundles $\mathcal L _{\lambda},\lambda \in X(\mathbf T)_+$, the group $ \mathbf G$ being simply connected. Now
$\langle {\mathcal X}_v, v\in W\rangle^\perp=0$ by Corollary \ref{cor:line_bundles-generation}.
 By Lemma \ref{lem:notorious} we get $\mathop{\mathrm D\kern0pt}\nolimits^b ({\mathrm{rep}} ({\mathbf B}))=\langle {\mathcal X}_v, v\in W\rangle$.

nodes.statement: Theorem is in fact a simple instance of base change for semiorthogonal decompositions, , which in this particular case can be stated in elementary terms. In more detail, consider a flat morphism picolon Xrightarrow S between smooth projective varieties, a closed point sin S and the base change diagram along the embedding i_scolon shookrightarrow S: [H] xymatrix @C5pc @R4pc X_sar[r]^iar@<-0.1ex>[d]_pi _s & X ar@<-0.4ex>[d]^pi \\ sar[r]^i_s & S Assume given an S-linear semiortogonal decomposition langle mathcal D _1,dots ,mathcal D _nrangle of mathopmathrm Dkern0ptnolimits ^b(X), such that each admissible subcategory mathcal D _i is equivalent to mathopmathrm Dkern0ptnolimits ^b(S). Then each embedding functor Phi _k:mathcal D _krightarrow mathopmathrm Dkern0ptnolimits ^b(X), k=1,dots,n is given by Phi _k(-)=(-)otimes E_k where E_k,k=1,dots n is a collection of objects of mathopmathrm Dkern0ptnolimits ^b(X) with the following two properties: 1) Rpi _astRmathcal Hom(E_i,E_j)=0 for i>j and 2) Rpi _astmathcal Hom(E_k,E_k)=mathcal O _S for all k (cf. Propositions and ). Restricting the objects E _kin mathopmathrm Dkern0ptnolimits ^b(X) to the fiber X_s, one obtains a collection of objects mathcal E _k:=i^astE_k, k=1,dots n. Now the claim is that the collection mathcal E _k, k=1,dots n is exceptional in mathopmathrm Dkern0ptnolimits ^b(X_s): for instance, to see that mathopRHomnolimits _X_s(mathcal E _i,mathcal E _j)=0 for i>j, by base change holds for the above Cartesian square, thus \ &mathopRHomnolimits _X_s(mathcal E _i,mathcal E _j)=Rpi _s_ast(mathcal E _i^astotimes ^mathbb Lmathcal E _j)=Rpi _s_asti^ast(E_i^astotimes ^mathbb LE _j)= \\ & i^ast_sRpi _ast(E_i^astotimes ^mathbb LE _j)=i^ast_sRpi _astRmathcal Hom(E_i,E_j)=0 by 1) above. Similarly for mathopRHomnolimits _X_s(mathcal E _i,mathcal E _i)=sf k for i=1,dots n. Finally, the objects mathcal E _i,i=1,dots n generate mathopmathrm Dkern0ptnolimits ^b(X_s): for if there was a non-trivial object mathcal F in langle mathcal E _1,dots ,mathcal E _nrangle ^perp, its pushforward i_s_astmathcal F in mathopmathrm Dkern0ptnolimits ^b(X) would be a non-trivial object in the right orthogonal to the semiortogonal decomposition langle mathcal D _1,dots ,mathcal D _nrangle of mathopmathrm Dkern0ptnolimits ^b(X), a contradiction.

\label{th:Pcoh-semi-orthogonal}Let $\mathcal D=\mathop{\mathrm D\kern0pt}\nolimits^b (\mathop{\sf {Coh}}\nolimits( \mathbf G / \mathbf P))$.
Let $v,w\in W^{\mathbf P}$.\\
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\mathop{\mathrm {Hom}}\nolimits_{\mathcal D}(\hat{\mathcal X}_v,\hat{\mathcal X}_v[i])=\begin{cases}{\sf k} &\text{if $i=0$},\\
0&\text{else.}\end{cases}$\\



\item If $w\succ  v$ then $\mathop{\mathrm {Hom}}\nolimits_{\mathcal D}(\hat{\mathcal X}_v,\hat{\mathcal X}_w[i])=0$ for all $i$.\\
\item The triangulated hull of $\{\hat{\mathcal X}_v\mid v \in W^{\mathbf P}\}$ is $\mathcal D$.
\end{enumerate}
In other words, the collection of objects $(\hat{\mathcal X}_v)_{v \in W^{\mathbf P}}$ is a full exceptional collection in $ \mathcal D$.

Let $\Pi^{\mathbf P}$ be the set of simple roots $\alpha$ for which $\mathbf P_\alpha\subset \mathbf P$.
Let $\Pi^{\notin \mathbf P}$ be the set of simple roots outside $\Pi^{\mathbf P}$.
We say that $\lambda$ is $\mathbf P$-dominant if $(\alpha^\vee,\lambda)\geq0$ for all $\alpha\in \Pi^{\mathbf P}$.
The set of $\mathbf P$-dominant weights is denoted $X^{\mathbf P}_+$.
Every $W_{\mathbf P}$-orbit of weights intersects $X^{\mathbf P}_+$ in a unique element.
Let $\mathbf G_{\mathbf P}$ be the semisimple subgroup of $\mathbf P$ with $\Pi^{\mathbf P}$ as simple roots. (So $\mathbf T\mathbf G_{\mathbf P}$ is a Levi subgroup $\mathbf L_{\mathbf P}$ of $\mathbf P$.)
Note that $\mathbf G_{\mathbf P}$ is simply connected.

We argue by induction along the well-ordered partial order $\leq_a$. So we assume the Theorem when $\tau$ is replaced by 
a $\sigma\in X_+^{\mathbf P}$ with $\sigma<_a\tau$. Let $\sigma\in X_+^{\mathbf P}$ with $\sigma<_a\tau$.
Thus $V\in {\mathcal S}$ when all weights $\xi$
of $V$ satisfy $\xi<_a\sigma$.

Step 1. First we  wish to show that ${\mathcal S}$ contains at least one $\mathbf P$-module $N$ with $N_\sigma={\sf k}_\sigma$ and with weights $\xi$
that satisfy $\xi\leq_a\sigma$.
If $\sigma$ is a Steinberg weight $e_v$, then $v\in W^{\mathbf P}$ by Lemma \ref{lem:PisP}
and we simply take $N=\hat M_v$.
If $\sigma$ is not a Steinberg weight,  then by Corollary \ref{cor:if not Steinberg then tensor}
 there is a fundamental weight $\omega_j$ and a weight $\mu$ with $(\mu,\mu)<(\sigma,\sigma)$,
 so that the $\mathbf B$-module $L=\nabla_{\omega_j}\otimes e^\mu$  has
$\sigma$ as a weight  of  multiplicity one, and so that all weights  $\nu$ of $L$ satisfy 
$\nu\leq_a\sigma$. Now take $N={\mathrm{ind}}_{\mathbf B}^{\mathbf P} L=\nabla_{\omega_j}\otimes{\mathrm{ind}}_{\mathbf B}^{\mathbf P} e^\mu$. 
By Lemma \ref{lem:indpreserve} every weight $\nu$ of $N$ satisfies $\nu\leq_a\sigma$ and 
$N_\sigma={\sf k}_\sigma$. In particular, ${\mathrm{ind}}_{\mathbf B}^{\mathbf P} e^\mu$ is nonzero, so  $\mu\in X^{\mathbf P}_+$ and ${\mathrm{ind}}_{\mathbf B}^{\mathbf P} e^\mu=\hat\nabla_\mu$.
And every weight $\nu$ of $\hat\nabla_\mu$ satisfies $(\nu,\nu)<(\sigma,\sigma)$, hence $\nu<_a\sigma$, so $\hat\nabla_\mu$  lies in ${\mathcal S}$ and  
$N=\nabla_{\omega_j}\otimes\hat\nabla_\mu$ lies in ${\mathcal S}$.

Step 2. Next we wish to show that $\hat\nabla_\sigma$ lies in ${\mathcal S}$. To this end we look for more $\mathbf P$-modules $N$ 
in ${\mathcal S}$ with $N_\sigma={\sf k}_\sigma$ 
and such that the weights $\xi$ of $N$
satisfy $\xi\leq_a\sigma$.
Start with the $N$ from Step 1.
Let $N^1$ be the span of the weight spaces $N_\mu$ with $(\mu,\omega_\alpha)<(\sigma,\omega_\alpha)$ for at least one
$\alpha\in \Pi^{\notin \mathbf P}$. Then $N^1$ is a $\mathbf P$-submodule that lies in ${\mathcal S}$. So we may replace $N$ with
$N/N^1$ and further assume $N^1=0$. 
Let $N^2$ be the span of the weight spaces $N_\mu$ with $(\mu,\omega_\alpha)\leq(\sigma,\omega_\alpha)$ for all
$\alpha\in \Pi^{\notin \mathbf P}$. Then $N^2$ is a $\mathbf P$-submodule and $N/N^2$ lies in ${\mathcal S}$. So we may replace $N$ with
$N^2$ and further assume $N^1=0$, $N=N^2$. 
Let $N^3$ be the $\mathbf P$-submodule of $N$ generated by $N_\sigma$.
Then $N/N^3$ is in ${\mathcal S}$, so we may replace $N$ with $N^3$. Now the unipotent radical of $\mathbf P$ acts trivially
on $N$ and the projection $p$ of $N$ onto its weight space $N_\sigma$ is $\mathbf T$-equivariant and $\mathbf G_{\mathbf P}$-equivariant,
hence $\mathbf P$-equivariant. By Lemma \ref{lem:indpreserve} the map $N\to \hat\nabla_\sigma$ induced by $p$ has kernel and cokernel in ${\mathcal S}$. So $\hat\nabla_\sigma$ lies  in ${\mathcal S}$.


Step 3.
Finally we want to show that ${\mathcal S}$ contains every  $\mathbf P$-module $V$ all whose weights $\mu$ satisfy $\mu<_a\tau$.
Consider such a $V$.
We may and shall assume  that ${\mathcal S}$ contains every  $\mathbf P$-module
 whose set of weights is a proper subset of the set of weights of $V$.
Say $V$ is nonzero. Choose an extremal weight $\sigma$ of $V$ that is $\mathbf P$-dominant.
Let $V^1$ be the span of the weight spaces $V_\mu$ with $(\mu,\omega_\alpha)<(\sigma,\omega_\alpha)$ for at least one
$\alpha\in \Pi^{\notin \mathbf P}$. This is a $\mathbf P$-submodule, and if $V^1$ is nonzero, then $V$ is in ${\mathcal S}$ because both
$V^1$ and $V/V^1$ are. 
Let $V^2$ be the span of the weight spaces $V_\mu$ with $(\mu,\omega_\alpha)\leq(\sigma,\omega_\alpha)$ for all
$\alpha\in \Pi^{\notin \mathbf P}$. This is a $\mathbf P$-submodule, and if $V^2\not= V$, then $V$ is in ${\mathcal S}$ because both
$V^2$ and $V/V^2$ are. 
So we further assume $V^1=0$ and $V=V^2$. Then  the unipotent radical of $\mathbf P$ acts trivially
on $V$. Let $V^3$ be the $\mathbf P$-submodule generated by $V_\sigma$.
If $V^3\not= V$, then $V$ is in ${\mathcal S}$ because both
$V^3$ and $V/V^3$ are. So we may assume $V=V^3$. The weights $\xi$ of $V$ now
satisfy $\xi\leq_a\sigma$.
The projection $p$ of $V$ onto its weight space $V_\sigma$ is $\mathbf T$-equivariant and $\mathbf G_{\mathbf P}$-equivariant,
hence $\mathbf P$-equivariant. We have  ${\mathrm{ind}}_{\mathbf B}^{\mathbf P}(V_\sigma)=\hat\nabla_\sigma\otimes (V_{\sigma})_{\mathrm{triv}}$, 
where $(V_{\sigma})_{\mathrm{triv}}$ is $V_{\sigma}$
with trivial $\mathbf P$-action, cf.\ \cite[Proposition 17]{FvdK}. Consider the map $f:V\to {\mathrm{ind}}_{\mathbf B}^{\mathbf P}(V_\sigma)=\hat\nabla_\sigma\otimes (V_{\sigma})_{\mathrm{triv}}$, corresponding with $p$. Both ${\mathsf{ker}}(f)$ and ${\mathsf{coker}}(f)$ lie in ${\mathcal S}$. 
As $\hat\nabla_\sigma$ lies in ${\mathcal S}$, so does $\hat\nabla_\sigma\otimes (V_{\sigma})_{\mathrm{triv}}$.
So $V$ lies in ${\mathcal S}$.

With these replacements in hand, we now proceed as in the case $\mathbf P=\mathbf B$:
For $p\in W^{\mathbf P}$, let $\hat X_p$ be the image of $P(-e_p)^*$ under the left adjoint of the inclusion of $\hat{\sf Q}_{\succeq p}$ 
into $\mathcal D=\mathop{\mathrm D\kern0pt}\nolimits ^b({\mathrm{rep}}( \mathbf P))$. 
And let $\hat Y_p$ be the image of $\hat Q(e_p)$ under the 
right adjoint of the inclusion of
$\hat{\sf P}_{\preceq p}$ into $\mathcal D$. 

Let $f_p$ be the natural map from $P(-e_p)^*$ to $Q(e_p)$. Recall that $f_p$ factors as a surjection $P(-e_p)^*\to{\sf k}_{e_p}$, followed by an injection ${\sf k}_{e_p}\to Q(e_p)$. Let $\hat f_p:P(-e_p)^*\to \hat Q(e_p)$ be induced by $f_p$. Then $\hat f_p$ induces an isomorphism of $\mathbf T$-modules 
$(P(-e_p)^*)_{e_p}\to (\hat Q(e_p))_{e_p}$ and the weights $\mu$ of ${\mathsf{ker}} (\hat f_p)$, ${\mathsf{coker}}(\hat f_p)$ satisfy $\mu<_a e_p$.
We have an exact triangle 
$$\dots \rightarrow \ker(\hat f_p)[1]\to {\mathsf{cone}}(\hat f_p)\to {\mathsf{coker}}(\hat f_p)\rightarrow \dots$$ in $\mathop{\mathrm D\kern0pt}\nolimits ^b({\mathrm{rep}}( \mathbf P))$.
Take $\hat M_v=Q(e_v)$ for $p\prec v\in W^{\mathbf P}$ and $\hat M_v=P(-e_v)^*$ for  $p\succ v\in W^{\mathbf P}$. It does not matter what we choose for $\hat M_p$ itself.

Using Theorem \ref{th:intervalgeneration} instead of Theorem \ref{th:cone generation}, we find that 
${\mathsf{cone}}(\hat f_p)$ lies in the triangulated hull of $\{\hat M_v\otimes \nabla_\lambda \mid v\in W^{\mathbf P},\ e_v <_a e_p,\ \lambda\in X(\mathbf T)_+\}$. 
So ${\mathsf{cone}}(\hat f_p)$ lies in the triangulated hull of $\hat{\sf P}_{\prec p}\cup\hat{\sf Q}_{\succ p}$.
One uses this to show that $\hat X_p$ and $\hat Y_p$ are isomorphic.
Mutatis mutandis the old constructions and proofs go through and 
Theorems \ref{th:Z-X^P_p-G-exceptional-coll}, \ref{th:Psemi-orthogonal}, \ref{th:Pcoh-semi-orthogonal} follow.

Let $X$ be a Frobenius split Fano $k$-variety such that ${\rm Pic}(X)=\mathbb Z$ with $\mathcal L\in {\rm Pic}(X)$ being the positive generator.
